1:
The verse divides the commentators before it has said anything else. Gill takes the words of the covenant to point forward rather than back — not to what goes before, but to what follows in the next chapters to the end of the book. Clarke goes the other way, and has the manuscripts with him: this verse seems properly to belong to the preceding chapter, since a widely different subject is taken up at the second verse, and it is distinguished as the sixty-ninth verse in some of the most correct copies of the Hebrew Bible. Ellicott knows that tradition and rejects it. The Hebrew Bibles do add this verse to the previous chapter and begin the new one at the second verse, but they cannot be right in so doing; the pronoun in Hebrew has nothing in it to determine whether it belongs to what precedes or to what follows, and the context settles the matter, since the covenant is described in the chapter that follows and not in the one that closes.

What was made in the land of Moab, all of them agree, was not a second covenant but the same one over again. Keil states the mechanism. The addresses of these two chapters are announced as words of the covenant which the Lord commanded Moses to make beside the covenant made at Horeb, and they consist in a renewed declaration of that covenant, or rather in a fresh obligation laid upon the nation to keep it; and there was no necessity for repeating the act itself, the offering of sacrifices and the sprinkling of the people with the sacrificial blood, because, notwithstanding the frequent transgressions of the nation, the covenant had never been abrogated on God's part but remained in full validity and force. Wesley says as much in a line — the covenant was but one in substance, though various in the time and manner of its dispensation. Clarke supplies the verb, that the word rendered make is lichroth, to cut, alluding to the covenant sacrifice offered on such an occasion and divided; and he holds what is instituted here to be an addition to the ten words given at Horeb, the curses denounced in this chapter differing from those denounced against transgressors of the decalogue.

Henry takes the renewal itself for the lesson. Moses, who was mediator before, is mediator still, and yet even Moses, king in Jeshurun though he was, could make the covenant no otherwise than as God gave him instructions: it does not lie in the power of ministers to fix the terms of the covenant, they are only to dispense the seals of it. Some then living had been old enough to consent for themselves at Horeb, and the covenant is renewed with them anyway — those that have solemnly covenanted with God should take all opportunities to do it again, as those that like their choice too well to change. But the far greater part were a new generation, and it is fit that the covenant should be renewed to the children of the covenant. Ellicott finds something larger in where the chapter stands. This covenant in the land of Moab lies outside the tremendous sanction appended to the expansion of the Sinaitic covenant, much as the chapter on vows in Leviticus lies outside the sanction that precedes it, vows not being compulsory; and the effect of that arrangement is that the curse is not the end of God's dealings with the chosen people. After it there is still another covenant, to the force of which there is no limit. The gifts and calling of God are irrevocable, nothing can destroy the relation between the Lord and Israel, and a watch in the night, in the psalm's phrase, is not the blackness of darkness for ever.
2:
Moses had been speaking to the heads of the people; now, Gill notes, he summoned the whole body together, a solemn covenant being about to be made. Keil reads all Israel the same way, the nation in all its members, and Ellicott draws out how wide that is: every rank is summoned, from the captains of the tribes down to the little ones and the lowest slaves, and the point set before them is one simple thing, to accept the Lord as their God. He notes that the pronoun is emphatic: yourselves are the witnesses, I need not repeat the story. Calvin puts the whole recital where it belongs, with the preface of the Law, since its tendency is to recommend the Law and to prepare the people's minds to be teachable. It begins from the divine blessings of the exodus and the wandering, for it would have been the height of baseness and ingratitude not to devote themselves to a Deliverer who had dealt so graciously with them; and it was an inestimable sign of his paternal love that he arrayed himself against so powerful a king for his servants' sake.

Then the sentence that has troubled every reader: yet the Lord hath not given you an heart to perceive. Gill and Ellicott both answer it from the rabbis, Ellicott quoting Rashi — a heart to mark the mercies of the Holy One and to cleave unto him. Clarke reports that some critics read the verse interrogatively, and hath not God given you a heart, on the ground that God could not reprehend them for failing in a duty when he had given them neither mind nor strength for it. The point is strictly just, Clarke allows, but the interrogation is unnecessary: the words imply only that they had not such a heart, not because God withheld the means of knowledge or the helps of his grace, but because they had not faithfully used them. Had they had such a heart it would have been God's gift, for he is the author of all good; that they had it not is proof they had grieved his Spirit. Calvin's figure is the one to keep — the drunken man, or one in a lethargy, who hears a cry, raises his head and opens his eyes a moment, then relapses into torpor.

Calvin does not stop at the diagnosis. A clear and powerful understanding is a special gift of the Spirit, since men are ever blind even in the brightest light until God has enlightened them; and yet the defect by no means frees us from blame, since every man's conscience convicts him that his ignorance is bound up with pride and indolence, and therefore voluntary. Wesley reaches the same balance by another road: their want of grace was their own fault and the just punishment of former sins, their case being like that of the men in Isaiah's day who first shut their own eyes, and then by God's righteous judgment had them closed; and God's readiness to do us good in other things is plain evidence that if we lack grace it is our own fault and not his. On the forty years the recital simply enumerates: clothes that did not wear out, a shoe that did not wear from the foot, and what Wesley calls heavenly and angelical bread. Clarke states the principle behind the list — they were not supported in an ordinary providential way, God working miracles continually that they might know him, and the means failed not because they were ill-calculated to answer his purpose but because the people were not workers with him. Ellicott catches the detail nobody else does: that they drank neither wine nor strong drink is a fact stated here only, and evidently comes from the lips of one who knew their walking through the wilderness.
10:
They stood, Gill says, gathered at the door of the tabernacle, or as Aben Ezra has it round about the ark, the symbol of the divine presence. Clarke gives the reason for the staging: a covenant implies two contracting parties, so God is represented as present while they and all their families, old and young, come before him. Keil reads the summons as one to enter inwardly, to make the covenant an affair of the heart and life, and notes that on that day the whole nation stood there without a single exception. He also corrects the rendering. The two members are parallel, the heads of the people being the elders and officers and the tribes consisting of all the men, so the Greek and Syriac reading, captains of your tribes, is at variance with the language. Ellicott needs one sentence for the point of it: there is no limit to the blessing of following the Lord and keeping his word, and it is open to all, from the highest to the lowest, to take hold of his covenant.

Henry and Calvin both walk the list of parties from the top down to the bottom, and Henry's descent is the one that keeps its edge. The great men must not think it any disparagement to their honour or diminution of their power to put their necks under the yoke of this covenant; rather they must enter first, to set a good example to their inferiors. The wives and children come in though they were never numbered or mustered, for even little ones are capable of being taken into covenant with God and are to be admitted with their parents. The stranger comes in, provided he had renounced all false gods — an early indication, Henry says, of favour to the Gentiles. And the hewers of wood and drawers of water come in, the meanest drudges among them: as none are too great to come under the bonds of the covenant, so none are too mean to inherit its blessings. Calvin runs the same ladder down to the very porters and baggage-carriers, and says why — so that the minds of those who derived their origin from the holy patriarchs should be the more solemnly impressed.

Both men press the oath. Henry hears God speaking in it: it is his oath, he has drawn it up and settled it, he has sworn to you and to him you must be sworn — which requires us to be sincere and serious, humble and reverent in our covenant transactions with him. Calvin turns it to the human side, that if perjury between man and man is detestable, much less pardonable is it to belie what you have promised God by his sacred name; and he adds the argument from antiquity, that God had prevented them by his grace many ages before they were born, so that not to embrace so signal a pledge of his love would have been very disgraceful. Then he raises the hard question himself. How could the little children pass into covenant, not being yet of an age to learn what it contained? The reply is easy. Though they did not receive the promised salvation by faith, nor renounce the flesh so as to dedicate themselves, they were bound by the same obligations their parents laid themselves under, since the grace was common to all; and coming of age they would endeavour after holiness the more cheerfully for remembering that they had already been dedicated to God. Circumcision was the sign of that adoption from the mother's womb, and infants are now initiated by baptism into the service of a God they do not yet know, because he claims them as his children when he engrafts them into the body of Christ.
11:
Gill notices what is unusual about the list before explaining anything: the little ones and the wives are scarce ever mentioned in any special law or solemn transaction, and here they stand named. Keil identifies the strangers historically — those who had attached themselves to Israel, the Egyptians who came out with them and the Midianites who joined with Hobab, down to the very lowest servant, from the hewer of wood to the drawer of water. Wesley qualifies the term the same way: such as had embraced their religion, all sorts of persons, yea even the meanest. Ellicott reaches for the two ends of the covenant's history. Behind this stands the promise to Abraham that the Almighty would be a God to him and to his seed, taking in the child of eight days old and the slave, who were to receive the sign of his covenant in their flesh; ahead of it stand Peter's words on the day of Pentecost, that the promise is unto you and to your children. From the hewer of wood Rashi infers that there were Canaanites who became proselytes in the time of Moses, in the same way as the Gibeonites in the days of Joshua.

The verb is the interesting thing at the verse following. It is not simply to enter but to pass, and Gill and Clarke both take it for an allusion to the old rite, Clarke setting the whole procedure out: the contracting parties, hitherto separate, meet in solemn assembly; a sacrifice is offered, the whole being a religious act; the victim is divided into two equal parts along the spine and the parts laid opposite each other with room between; the parties meet in the victim, the conditions are recited, and an oath is taken by which the covenant is ratified. Ellicott is not so sure. Rashi illustrates the word from Jeremiah in just that way, and there is the prophet's own image of passing under the rod into its bond; but no such ceremony is mentioned here, and we can only say that the practice may possibly have given occasion for this use of the word. On the oath he is more definite: the word appears here for the first time in Deuteronomy and is rendered curse later in this same chapter, and it seems to mean an imprecation in the name of God which may bring a curse if the thing sworn to is not fulfilled.

Ellicott's note on the verse after carries furthest. This, he says, is the aspect of the covenant that makes the Lord responsible for the fulfilment of the whole — he takes all this trouble, in Rashi's phrase, for the sake of establishing thee in his presence for a people — and the people's part, as described here, is only to accept the position. That brings the Moab transaction into the closest similarity with what the prophet and the epistle call the new covenant, whose form is that I will be to them a God and they shall be to me a people. God undertakes for the people's part as well as his own: the first half appears here, that he may be unto thee a God, and the second in the chapter following, where the Lord will circumcise thy heart to love him. Keil gives the same clause its plainer sense, that he may set thee up, exalt thee, into a people for himself. Wesley takes it for the summary of the whole — that they should be established for a people to him, to fear and love and obey and be devoted to him, and that he should be to them a God, to make them holy and happy; and a due sense of the relation we stand in to him is enough to bring us to all the duties and all the comforts of it.
14:
Moses does not make the covenant with the men in front of him only, and the commentators are unanimous on who else is in it, Clarke stating it in a line: him that standeth here is the present generation, him that is not here is all future generations of this people. Gill gives Aben Ezra's version, not only you but those that will come after you, your sons and your sons' sons. Keil widens it further than either. The covenant was made with all, whether present or not, and was to embrace not only those living then but their descendants, so as to become a covenant of blessing for all nations — which is why he hears behind it both Peter's promise to you and to your children, and the intercession of Christ for those who should believe through the apostles' word.

Wesley works the point out at length, and by an argument from ordinary law. The covenant was made at first with Abraham and his seed, and as God engaged himself to continue the blessing of Abraham upon his posterity, so he engaged them to the same duties that were required of Abraham. So it is even among men: where a king confers an estate upon a subject and his heirs for ever upon certain conditions, all his heirs who enjoy that benefit are obliged to the same conditions. He allows that the phrase may take in those constrained to be absent by sickness or necessary occasion, and then reports the boldest reading of all, from one of the Chaldee paraphrasts — all the generations that have been from the first days of the world, and all that shall arise to the end of the whole world, stand with us here this day. Taking the transaction as a typical dispensation of the covenant of grace, Wesley finds in that a noble testimony to the Mediator of it, who is the same yesterday, today and for ever.

Then the reason for renewing it now. Gill counts the years — upwards of two hundred in a country much given to idolatry, where they had seen many of its idols and much of its worship, so that their hearts had been apt to be ensnared and some minds tinctured with it, and the remembrance might yet make ill impressions on them. Wesley says as much more bluntly, that they had learned too much of those idolatries, as the golden calf shewed; and he adds the other half of the debt, that there also they were in dreadful bondage, whence God alone delivered them. Of the march itself he says only, with what hazard, if God had not appeared for us. Calvin looks forward rather than back. We know how greatly men's minds are tickled by novelty, and on entering Canaan they would meet many forms of idolatry hitherto unknown, so many snares to entangle them; so Moses exhorts them to beware by former instances, since they knew by extraordinary proofs that whatever imaginations the heathen nations had invented were hateful to God. The argument is drawn from experience. Keil puts that experience in a word: what they had learned of the idols of those nations was that they are not gods at all, but only wood and stone — gillulim, which means literally clods.
17:
Gill will not let the word for idols pass politely. It has the signification of dung, and may be rendered dunghill gods — either because some were bred and lived in dung, as Bishop Patrick says of the beetle the Egyptians worshipped, or simply because they were as loathsome as dung. Then the root that beareth gall and wormwood, on which Keil supplies the botany: rosh is a plant of very bitter taste, commonly coupled with wormwood, and though not strictly poisonous it makes a striking image of the destructive fruit borne by idolatry. Ellicott sets the clause in the argument — I make this covenant binding upon all your generations in case there should even now be some root of idolatry among you which may bear fruit in later times and bring a curse upon the country; and that there were such roots is only too plain from what followed after the elders of that generation died. Clarke identifies the root with the apostle's evil heart of unbelief departing from the living God, allowing that it may mean false doctrines or idolatrous persons too.

Calvin reads the root as something more interior. By the word he understands the hidden principles of sins, which unless prevented in good time spring up with collected vigour and lift themselves on high, since indulgence in sin increases by concealment and connivance; He notices too that Moses passes from man and woman to family and tribe, so that those associated with others in sin excuse themselves in vain by their numbers: a whole nation is as much to be condemned as a single person. On the man who blesses himself in his heart Calvin is sharper still. To bless oneself is to hope in one's secret imaginations that all will go well, as hypocrites do, who in their foolish self-adulation applaud themselves deceitfully lest they should hear God thundering; and nothing is worse than to hope for peace while we wage war with God. Wesley puts it plainly: the man flatters himself in his own eyes with vain hopes, as if God did not mind such things and either could not or would not punish them. Ellicott corrects the word that carries it — not the imagination of his heart but the stubbornness of it.

The last clause of that verse divides everybody, and admits at least three readings. Wesley would reverse it, to add thirst to drunkenness: when the man has multiplied his sins and made himself as it were drunk with them he is still not satisfied, but whets his appetite for more, as drunkards contrive to make themselves thirsty again. Calvin takes it the other way, as a proverbial figure: Moses forbids us to excite appetites already heated by new stimulants, as those do who add oil to a fire already lit; lust in a man is like an insatiable dropsy. Ellicott records a third, from the Greek, which turns the sentence into a plea — that one idolater would not make much difference to Israel, that the drunkard could not be the ruin of the thirsty, and so a man might do as he pleased and escape punishment, protected by the general prosperity of the nation. The warning in Hebrews, he says, meets that mistaken view admirably. The sentence itself allows no such shelter. Calvin holds that the obstinacy in which the wicked are wilfully hardened shuts against them the door of hope, since the man who abandons himself to sin expecting impunity has not only extinguished the light of his own reason but dethroned God, as if he were not the Judge of the world. Ellicott hears the verdict in the verbs: the anger that shall smoke, as Sinai was altogether on a smoke when the Lord descended in fire, and the curses that shall lie upon him as beasts lie down in their lairs.
22:
Calvin explains why the question gets asked at all. The punishments would be no ordinary ones, such as fall into contempt from their common use, but like portents; the question put here refers to something extraordinary and not easily comprehended. It looks back over the whole list of curses, not that each by itself would awaken such horror, but that heaped one upon another, by their number and severity and duration, they compelled men to wonder. Everywhere men are afflicted with diseases, and barrenness for a season is a common evil; but that sickness should cleave as it were to the marrow of a whole people, and the earth be dried up as if burnt with sulphur, is an awful spectacle in which God's vengeance, which else would be incredible, manifestly appears. Gill dates the asking late — not the next generation but future ages, even after the destruction of Judea by the Romans. Ellicott sets the two descriptions of the land side by side: can this be the same country of which it was written that it is a land of brooks of water, of wheat and barley and vines, a land the Lord thy God careth for? Everyone knows which description has been nearer the fact for many centuries.

The answer, when it comes, turns on a phrase the translators have handled badly. Gods whom he had not given unto them is, Clarke says flatly, an unhappy rendering; Houbigant makes it gods with whom they had no society, and falls unmercifully on Le Clerc for making it gods from whom they had received no benefit. Clarke differs from both, because the word signifies a portion or inheritance, and God is frequently represented in scripture as the portion of his people; so the line should read that there was no portion to them — the gods they served could neither supply their wants nor save their souls. Ellicott arrives independently at the same sense, that none of them gave the people any portion. Wesley keeps the received rendering and finds another meaning in it: God had not given those gods to Israel for their worship, but had divided them unto all nations for their use and service — the sun and moon and stars, the principal gods of the neighbouring nations.

Keil reads the reply as ending in submission rather than explanation, closing with the confession that what is hidden belongs to the Lord and what is revealed to us and to our children. Gill hears the rooting out as fulfilled twice over, at the Babylonish captivity and again by the Romans, and marks the difference: at the end of seventy years they returned from Babylon, whereas from the later dispersion, he writes, they have not been able to return these seventeen hundred years. Calvin will allow them no excuse for it. Moses amplifies the crime when he says that, forsaking the God of their fathers, their deliverer, who had covenanted with them, they served strange and unknown gods from whom they had received no benefit; there could be no pretence of ignorance, for God had bound them to himself both by his word and by the incomparable manifestation of his power. Let us learn from it, Calvin adds, anxiously to inquire who the true God is and what he wills, since there is no true religion without knowledge. Henry ends where the chapter cannot: it is no new thing for God to bring desolating judgments on a people near to him in profession, and he never does it without good reason; but the law of Moses leaves sinners under the curse and rooted out of the Lord's land, whereas the grace of Christ toward penitent believing sinners plants them again in their land, and they shall no more be pulled up, being kept by the power of God.
29:
The verse is so concise that its meaning has always been disputed, and Calvin clears two readings away before offering his own. Some of the Hebrews, Aben Ezra among them, take it of punishment: secret sins belong to God, that he may punish them, while sins publicly done belong to us to punish. Forced, says Calvin, since punishment is not the subject here — Moses is commending the use of the doctrine of the Law. Others read it as praising the Law for making God's secret things known, which would be likelier if the grammar allowed it; but the demonstrative prefix on both clauses, and the copula between them, forbid running them together. Clarke rejects a third, Houbigant's rendering that the things hidden with the Lord are made manifest to us and our children for many generations: none of the ancient versions, he finds, understood it so. Ellicott records Rashi's reading, which ties the secret things to the secret idolater earlier in the chapter: wilt thou punish the many for the devices of one, when no man knows the secrets of his fellow?

Calvin's own reading takes the copula adversatively. God indeed retains to himself secret things, which it neither concerns nor profits us to know; but what he has declared belongs to us and to our children. He calls it a remarkable passage, condemning audacity and curiosity while rousing pious minds to seek instruction. Men are anxious to understand what it is unprofitable and even injurious to investigate; all would be God's counsellors and penetrate the deepest recesses of heaven — nought for mortals is too high, as the heathen poet has it, our folly reaches to the sky — while what God plainly sets before us is neglected, or turned from in disgust. Gill fills in what the hidden things are: much in nature that finite minds cannot account for, much in providence past finding out, and much in God himself that revelation has not opened — not only perfections such as eternity and immensity, but the mode of subsistence of the three Persons. Wesley reads the exclamation as pastoral rather than doctrinal, spoken either to bridle a curiosity that would ask the time and manner of the judgment, or to quiet those who, seeing God deal so severely with his own people while sparing nations guilty of grosser idolatry, might take occasion to deny his providence.

What is revealed is another matter. Clarke states the balance: what God has thought proper to reveal is essential to the well-being of man, and intended not for one time or one people but for all succeeding generations, while what he has not revealed concerns God alone and is not to be inquired after. He notes too that the Jews have always held these words of the highest importance, affixing marks in the original to the phrase to us and to our children. Ellicott will not stop there. Moses was delivering not law only but prophecy, and there was more in this part of it than he himself could understand. Must he not have longed to know what would befall his people in the latter days? All those curses were to come upon Israel, and after them there was still a covenant embracing every generation to the world's end; and if we, upon whom the ends of the world are come, do not yet see Israel's future distinctly, the words are appropriate still. Henry sets the ending beside Paul's, who closed his discourse on the same subject when it had begun to be fulfilled. God has kept back nothing profitable for us, but only that of which it is good for us to be ignorant; and the end of all divine revelation is not to furnish curious subjects of speculation, but that we may do all the words of this law and be blessed in our deed.
